Other moderation records
Automatic link removals, self-harm removals and automation runs keep the message text only so moderators can review what happened.
The message text is deleted 30 days after the event, unless an open appeal needs it. The case outcome, dates and scores stay.
The code prints the text of every message

Every message AutoMod sees, in every server, is printed with its full text to the bot's output, and nothing in the code turns this off. Under the Docker setup in AutoMod's self-hosting guide, that output would be saved to a log file with no size limit. AutoMod's developer has since told us these logs are a debugging feature and aren't kept on the official instance.

AutoMod's support server carries Stoat's verified badge, its developer is on the Stoat team, and its README calls it "Stoat's premier moderation bot". Yet its website, docs and source code have no privacy policy, terms or privacy notice, so members can't find out what it collects, how long it keeps it or how to ask for deletion. Its developer has told us Stoat has asked for one and that it's being prepared with legal advice.

Bridging without member consent

A server owner can bridge a channel to Discord and Fluxer with !bridge. Kuma's privacy policy says it then copies members' messages, "their text, attachments, and your username and avatar", to the other platforms. The only control it mentions is that "bridging is off until an admin sets it up". We found no notice to members, consent step or opt-out in its policy or command help, so this raises the same consent question as bolt.

Per-person activity history

Each person's daily message, edit, delete and command counts are stored for every server and every channel until they opt out or the bot leaves. Stoat's latest guidance allows this kind of data to be kept that long, but says counts tied to a person are user data that need opt-in.

Anyone can run .stats top g to rank the most active people across every server bronx is in, even outside a server. People are ranked whether or not they've ever used bronx, unless they've opted out. Stoat says cross-server rankings fall under a bot's general opt-in.

Application answers are stored with the applicant's user ID and no deletion deadline. Stoat's latest guidance says content like this should be kept for 30 days unless there's a specific reason to keep it longer. Stoatmod deletes applications after 14 days.
Messages relayed to other platforms
When an admin bridges a channel, bronx relays members' messages, names and avatars to another platform. Members get no notice or choice before their messages leave the server.
Per-person statistics: are message, edit, delete and command counts tied to a user ID allowed?
You can store these yes, but if they are tied to a user then they must be considered user data/user statistics and not generic statistics, and would fall under #4.
Opt-in or opt-out: is a one-command opt-out enough, or is opt-in required?
At this time we're asking everyone to use opt-in. This may be changed/become more nuanced in future developer policies.
Cross-server rankings: is a leaderboard across every server allowed?
I would say this falls under your general data collection opt in, though offering the option to opt out of that feature specifically may be nice (this isn't a requirement, just a personal opinion).
Retention: how long can activity stats, command logs, edit and delete history, and applications be kept?

Data that contains PII (eg. message content, attachments) should be kept for 30 days unless there is an explicit reason to keep it further (eg. moderation case that is being appealed at 29 days). Other operational data may be kept as long as it is relevant (The longest period would likely be until the bot is removed from the server).
Bridges: does an admin setting up a bridge count as authorisation, or do members need notice or to consent?
Tbh we're still discussing policy on bridge bots, I don't have an answer on this currently.
Privacy policies: will they be mandatory for every bot that handles user data?
We would like bots to have privacy policies. I can confirm this will be a requirement with our new policies.
Developer guidelines: is there a timeline, and will existing bots get time to comply?
In the works yes, no timeline atm. [...] yes there will be a migration period.
Everyone is counted per person, automatically

Every message is counted against the sender's user ID from the moment bronx joins. Only the number is stored, not what was said. Server-wide totals would be anonymous, but these counts are tied to each person and used to rank them.
Members can opt out, but aren't asked first

bronx's privacy page lets anyone download their data or opt out, which deletes their records and stops future tracking. The code supports this: messages from an opted-out user are dropped before bronx counts them. But nobody is asked before counting starts, and Stoat has since said it's asking every bot to use opt-in.
bronx privacy page
Its privacy page says nothing is collected passively
The privacy page says "nothing is collected passively — data is only written when you interact with a feature". The code counts every message a person sends, whether or not they've ever used bronx.
main.cpp#L1011
The stats commands are open to every member. They show who sends the most messages in a server, and across all servers with the global option. People are listed unless they've opted out.

In line with Stoat's latest guidance

Stoat has since said message content should be kept for 30 days unless there's a specific reason to keep it longer, such as a moderation case being appealed at 29 days. That's the schedule above. See “Stoat's latest guidance” in section 06 for the full answers.

When Stoatmod is removed from a server, we delete everything we hold for that server, except network-level enforcement records such as a server blacklist entry. This matches Stoat's guidance that other data can be kept until the bot is removed.

Join verification and the report form still use Cloudflare Turnstile as a browser CAPTCHA, but only after the person agrees: it doesn't load until they tick the agreement. Kuma has dropped Cloudflare from its Stoat verification, which we see as a step in the right direction. Stoat has not objected to us continuing to use it where the person consents.

We raised log_it and AutoMod with Stoat because of what their public docs seemed to describe when we looked. We looked at bronx, a group of three bots by one developer, bolt and Kuma later. AutoMod, bronx and bolt are open source, so we also read their code to check what they actually do. The code for log_it, Kuma and the group of three bots isn't public, so for those we relied on what their own websites and profiles say. These examples are here to show why a platform-wide answer is needed, not to accuse anyone.

To be fair to AutoMod, we found no per-person activity stats, no sharing between servers and no messages sent to an outside AI service. Its main gap is that it doesn't yet tell members what it collects or how long it keeps it.

Stoat required us to get each person's consent before their content was sent to an outside service, and told us that neither a server owner's choice nor a privacy policy counts as consent. A bridge sends members' messages to other platforms on the strength of an admin's choice and a privacy policy alone. If the rule we were held to applies to every bot, bridged channels need a way for each member to agree before their messages are sent off Stoat. Stoat has since told another developer it's still deciding its policy on bridge bots.

Update, 14 October 2026: Kuma has rebuilt its verification on Stoat

Kuma says the changes bring its verification in line with Stoat's guidelines. Its announcement says Stoat verification no longer checks IP addresses, VPNs or anything about a member's connection, that hashed IP addresses from earlier verifications have been deleted, that Kuma's own browser check replaces the Cloudflare captcha, and that Raid Guard no longer uses other servers' reports on Stoat. Discord and Fluxer verification are unchanged.

That answers the first two findings above, which describe what we read on 6 October. We welcome it, and we see Kuma dropping Cloudflare Turnstile as a step in the right direction. Our own join verification and report form still use Turnstile, but it only loads after the person agrees, and Stoat has not objected to us continuing to use it where the person consents.
